Olympic firsts.Women compete: Charlotte Cooper won the first tennis title, making her the first individual female Olympic champion, in Paris in 1900.
Olympic firsts.Gold, silver and bronze: Before this, winners received silver, and the St. Louis Games introduced the three-medal podium.
Olympic firsts.Olympic rings flag flies: Pierre de Coubertin designed the five interlocking rings, and they first flew at the Games in Antwerp.
Olympic firsts.Olympic flame burns: Amsterdam placed a flame in a tower, but the relay carrying a torch from Greece did not yet exist.
Olympic firsts.First torch relay: The Berlin relay carried fire from Olympia, Greece, and was a Nazi propaganda spectacle, though the tradition survives.
Olympic firsts.Games south of the equator: Horse events were held in Stockholm because Australian quarantine rules blocked the horses, at the Melbourne Games.
Olympic firsts.Games in Asia: Tokyo introduced judo to the Olympics, and the Games were broadcast by satellite.
Olympic firsts.Official mascot (Waldi): Munich's cheerful dachshund, designed in rainbow colors, was the first official Olympic mascot.
Olympic firsts.Games in South America: The Rio Games were the first held on the continent, and this made South America the last inhabited continent to host.
Olympic firsts.Full gender parity: Paris offered equal numbers of male and female athletes, a first for the Games.

Distance from Cape Town.Johannesburg: Johannesburg was founded in 1886 after gold was found on the Witwatersrand, and it grew into South Africa's largest city.
Distance from Cape Town.Harare: Harare was called Salisbury until 1982. It stands on a high plateau, which gives it a mild climate.
Distance from Cape Town.Nairobi: Nairobi began in 1899 as a railway depot on the Uganda line. Its name comes from the Maasai for 'cool water'.
Distance from Cape Town.Rio de Janeiro: Rio and Cape Town face each other across the South Atlantic, and both are dominated by iconic peaks, Sugarloaf and Table Mountain.
Distance from Cape Town.Cairo: The Great Pyramid of Giza, near Cairo, was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for around 3,800 years.
Distance from Cape Town.Perth: Perth is often called the world's most isolated major city, since the nearest city of comparable size is Adelaide, about 2,100 km away.
Distance from Cape Town.London: The Cape was called the 'Tavern of the Seas' because Dutch East India Company ships stopped for fresh supplies on the way to Asia.
Distance from Cape Town.Sydney: Sydney's Harbour Bridge, nicknamed 'the Coathanger', opened in 1932, and the harbor is one of the world's largest natural harbors.
Distance from Cape Town.New York: New York is about 12,500 km from Cape Town, a flight of roughly 15 hours, and one of the longest routes in the world.
Distance from Cape Town.Tokyo: Greater Tokyo is home to around 37 million people, the largest urban area on Earth.

Milestones in mathematics.Euclid's Elements: This textbook of geometry was used in classrooms for over 2,000 years and is among the most reprinted books in history.
Milestones in mathematics.Zero as a number (Brahmagupta): Brahmagupta's Indian text was among the first to give rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying with zero and negative numbers.
Milestones in mathematics.Al-Khwarizmi's algebra: His book gave algebra its name from al-jabr, and the Latinized form of his own name gave us the word algorithm.
Milestones in mathematics.Fibonacci's Liber Abaci: Leonardo of Pisa brought Hindu-Arabic numerals to Europe and posed a rabbit-breeding puzzle that gave us the Fibonacci sequence.
Milestones in mathematics.Napier's logarithms: A Scottish laird invented them, turning multiplication into addition, and they powered slide rules for about 350 years.
Milestones in mathematics.Calculus (Newton, Leibniz): The two worked independently and then fought a bitter priority dispute, but Leibniz's notation is the one still used in textbooks.
Milestones in mathematics.Euler's identity: The formula e to the iπ plus 1 equals 0 ties together five of math's most important constants and is often voted the most beautiful equation.
Milestones in mathematics.Non-Euclidean geometry: Lobachevsky and Bolyai showed geometries where Euclid's parallel postulate fails, math that Einstein later used to describe curved spacetime.
Milestones in mathematics.Gödel's incompleteness: Kurt Gödel proved that any consistent system of arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, and he was only 25.
Milestones in mathematics.Fermat's Last Theorem proved: Andrew Wiles solved a puzzle Fermat had scribbled in a margin in 1637, after about seven years of working on it in secret.

Corporate landmarks, by completion year.Woolworth Building: The Woolworth Building was the world's tallest at its time, and it was nicknamed the Cathedral of Commerce.
Corporate landmarks, by completion year.Chrysler Building: The Chrysler Building's stainless steel spire was assembled secretly inside the building, and it briefly became the world's tallest.
Corporate landmarks, by completion year.Seagram Building: The Seagram Building is a masterpiece of modernism, designed by Mies van der Rohe, and its bronze facade is famous.
Corporate landmarks, by completion year.Sears Tower: The Sears Tower was the world's tallest building for about 25 years, and it is now renamed Willis Tower.
Corporate landmarks, by completion year.Citigroup Center: The Citigroup Center sits on stilts, and engineers discovered a structural flaw after construction, and quietly repaired it.
Corporate landmarks, by completion year.Lloyd's building, London: Lloyd's building has its pipes and lifts on the outside, and it was designed by Richard Rogers, who also designed the Pompidou Centre.
Corporate landmarks, by completion year.Bank of China Tower: The Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong is shaped like a series of triangles, and was designed by I. M. Pei.
Corporate landmarks, by completion year.Petronas Towers: The Petronas Towers were the world's tallest buildings until 2004, and they are linked by a skybridge.
Corporate landmarks, by completion year.The Gherkin (Swiss Re): The Gherkin is a London landmark, and it has a distinctive curved shape that is energy efficient.
Corporate landmarks, by completion year.Apple Park: Apple Park is a huge ring-shaped campus in Cupertino, and it is covered in glass and powered by renewables.

Great museums, by founding year.British Museum: Collector Sir Hans Sloane's 71,000 objects formed its foundation, making it the first national public museum in the world.
Great museums, by founding year.The Hermitage: Catherine the Great began it with a purchase of paintings, and the museum is still home to dozens of resident cats.
Great museums, by founding year.The Louvre (as museum): A medieval fortress and royal palace before becoming a museum in the Revolution, it gained its glass pyramid entrance in 1989.
Great museums, by founding year.Museo del Prado: It holds the finest collections of Goya and Velazquez, including Las Meninas, in the world.
Great museums, by founding year.National Gallery, London: It was founded when Parliament bought 38 paintings from banker John Julius Angerstein, and it overlooks Trafalgar Square.
Great museums, by founding year.Metropolitan Museum of Art: Its two million works include an entire Egyptian temple, the Temple of Dendur, rebuilt inside the museum.
Great museums, by founding year.Tate: Funded by sugar magnate Henry Tate, its original Millbank building is now known as Tate Britain.
Great museums, by founding year.MoMA: It opened days after the 1929 stock market crash and now holds Van Gogh's The Starry Night.
Great museums, by founding year.Centre Pompidou: Its pipes and ducts are on the outside, colour-coded, in a radical design by Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers.
Great museums, by founding year.Guggenheim Bilbao: Frank Gehry's titanium-clad building revitalised a post-industrial city, giving rise to the term Bilbao effect.

US Monopoly spaces, going round from GO.Mediterranean Avenue: The cheapest property, paired with Baltic Avenue, is named for a real street in Atlantic City.
US Monopoly spaces, going round from GO.Income Tax: In older editions, players chose between paying 10 percent of their wealth or a flat $200.
US Monopoly spaces, going round from GO.Reading Railroad: It is pronounced Redding, after the real Pennsylvania railroad, and it is one of four railroads on the board.
US Monopoly spaces, going round from GO.Jail: You sit here or just visit, and rolling doubles three times in a row also sends you directly there.
US Monopoly spaces, going round from GO.Electric Company: One of two utilities, its rent depends on a dice roll, and owning both raises the multiplier.
US Monopoly spaces, going round from GO.Free Parking: Official rules give nothing here, but many families add a house rule that gives players a jackpot.
US Monopoly spaces, going round from GO.B. and O. Railroad: The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, chartered in 1827, was among the first common-carrier railroads in the US.
US Monopoly spaces, going round from GO.Go to Jail: This corner sends you straight to jail without collecting $200 for passing Go.
US Monopoly spaces, going round from GO.Pacific Avenue: The first of the green properties, it is named for a real avenue in Atlantic City.
US Monopoly spaces, going round from GO.Luxury Tax: This $75 charge is the last stop before Boardwalk, so the end of the lap can be pricey.

Household products, by launch year.Vaseline: Vaseline began when Robert Chesebrough noticed oil workers using the gooey residue from rigs to heal cuts and burns, then refined and sold it.
Household products, by launch year.Ivory soap: Ivory soap's famous claim of being 99 and 44/100 percent pure arrived soon after a legend that a worker's mixing mistake made it float.
Household products, by launch year.Lysol: Lysol was first sold as a disinfectant, and ads in the early 20th century even pitched it for personal hygiene, which was both useless and risky.
Household products, by launch year.Gillette safety razor: King Camp Gillette's disposable-blade idea made money by selling the razor cheaply and the replaceable blades repeatedly, a model still copied today.
Household products, by launch year.Clorox bleach: Clorox started as a factory in Oakland, California, whose founders made industrial bleach from brine before the product reached homes.
Household products, by launch year.Windex: Windex first hit shelves in a spray bottle, and its blue color was added later so the liquid would be easy to recognize.
Household products, by launch year.Tide: Tide was marketed as the first heavy-duty synthetic detergent and transformed washing because it did not leave a gray soap scum.
Household products, by launch year.Pampers: Pampers began after Procter & Gamble engineer Vic Mills, frustrated with cloth diapers while caring for his grandchild, designed a disposable one.
Household products, by launch year.Swiffer: The Swiffer popularized the idea of a disposable cleaning cloth on a handle, changing how many homes sweep and dust.
Household products, by launch year.Tide Pods: Tide Pods became notorious when a viral challenge led some teens to bite them, prompting warnings and a redesigned, harder-to-open container.

Capitals of the Americas by elevation.Buenos Aires: Buenos Aires sits only a few meters above the Río de la Plata, which is why its ground is flat and low-lying.
Capitals of the Americas by elevation.Ottawa: Ottawa is on the Ottawa River at the border of Ontario and Quebec, and was picked as capital partly because it was between English and French Canada.
Capitals of the Americas by elevation.Santiago: Santiago lies in a valley between the Andes and the Coastal Range, and smog gets trapped there on still days.
Capitals of the Americas by elevation.Caracas: Caracas sits in a valley, around 900 meters high, but near the coast, so it has a mild climate all year round, known as 'the city of eternal spring'.
Capitals of the Americas by elevation.Brasília: Brasília was built from scratch in the 1950s on a high plateau, and its layout was shaped like an airplane.
Capitals of the Americas by elevation.Guatemala City: Guatemala City sits in a highland valley, ringed by volcanoes, and has a mild climate all year.
Capitals of the Americas by elevation.Mexico City: Mexico City is built on a drained lake bed, which is why it sinks and why its earthquakes are amplified.
Capitals of the Americas by elevation.Bogotá: Bogotá lies on a high plateau in the Andes, and it has a mild but cool climate, which locals say needs a jacket year round.
Capitals of the Americas by elevation.Quito: Quito is among the highest capitals in the world and sits only about 25 km from the equator, so its altitude keeps it cool.
Capitals of the Americas by elevation.La Paz: La Paz, in Bolivia, is the world's highest seat of government, and a cable-car network carries commuters up and down its canyon walls.

Scientific notation: which is biggest?.7 × 10^1: Seventy years is close to today's global life expectancy, a handy yardstick at the small end of this list.
Scientific notation: which is biggest?.1.2 × 10^2: Jeanne Calment of France, the oldest verified person ever, lived to 122, just beyond this number of years.
Scientific notation: which is biggest?.Nine hundred fifty: Spelled-out numbers hide their size; converted to 9.5 × 10^2, it slots in neatly between the smaller and larger values.
Scientific notation: which is biggest?.2 × 10^3: A US short ton is 2,000 pounds, and notably different from the metric tonne of 1,000 kg.
Scientific notation: which is biggest?.4.8 × 10^3: Mont Blanc, the highest peak in the Alps, stands about 4,806 m above sea level, close to this number.
Scientific notation: which is biggest?.Ten thousand minus one: The trap here is that it's one short of 10^4, so it loses to the 1 × 10^4 below it by exactly one.
Scientific notation: which is biggest?.1 × 10^4: The Greeks called 10,000 a 'myrias', the biggest number with its own word, which is where English gets 'myriad'.
Scientific notation: which is biggest?.3.5 × 10^4: Airliners cruise at roughly 35,000 feet, where the air is thin and cold enough to cut drag and save fuel.
Scientific notation: which is biggest?.0.9 × 10^5: The trap: proper scientific notation needs a leading figure from 1 up to 10, so this really means 9 × 10^4.
Scientific notation: which is biggest?.1.1 × 10^5: A typical human scalp carries around 100,000 hairs, close to this number, though redheads have fewer and blondes more.

Apollo 11, step by step.Saturn V liftoff: The first stage burned through roughly 2,000 tonnes of propellant in under three minutes, and the launch was felt miles away.
Apollo 11, step by step.Reaching Earth orbit: Orbit took only about 12 minutes, after which the crew circled Earth once and a half before the big burn toward the Moon.
Apollo 11, step by step.Trans-lunar injection burn: The third stage fired for about six minutes, accelerating the crew to nearly 39,000 kilometres per hour on the way to the Moon.
Apollo 11, step by step.Entering lunar orbit: A burn behind the Moon, out of radio contact with Earth, slowed them into orbit, and they circled the Moon 30 times.
Apollo 11, step by step.Eagle touches down: Armstrong took manual control to avoid a boulder field and landed with under a minute of fuel left: 'The Eagle has landed.'
Apollo 11, step by step.Armstrong's first step: About 600 million people watched on live TV as Armstrong stepped out first, and he meant to say 'a man', not just 'man'.
Apollo 11, step by step.US flag planted: The flag had a horizontal rod so it appeared to fly in the airless air; Aldrin said the exhaust blast knocked it over at departure.
Apollo 11, step by step.Eagle lifts off the Moon: A broken circuit-breaker switch nearly stranded them, and Aldrin is said to have used a felt-tip pen to push in the ignition.
Apollo 11, step by step.Re-entry into the atmosphere: The capsule hit the atmosphere at about 11 kilometres per second, and its heat shield endured temperatures of thousands of degrees.
Apollo 11, step by step.Splashdown in the Pacific: The capsule landed near the USS Hornet, and the crew then spent 21 days in quarantine, in case they had brought back lunar germs.

Whose face is on it? US money by value.Lincoln (on a coin): It was the first US circulation coin to carry a real person's portrait, issued for Lincoln's centennial in 1909.
Whose face is on it? US money by value.Jefferson (on a coin): The back of the nickel shows Monticello, Jefferson's own home.
Whose face is on it? US money by value.Franklin D. Roosevelt: His face was chosen after his death in 1945, tied to the March of Dimes polio charity.
Whose face is on it? US money by value.Washington (on a coin): It was introduced in 1932 to mark the 200th anniversary of his birth.
Whose face is on it? US money by value.John F. Kennedy: It was issued in 1964, within months of his assassination.
Whose face is on it? US money by value.Sacagawea: The Shoshone woman who guided Lewis and Clark is shown carrying her infant son.
Whose face is on it? US money by value.Alexander Hamilton: The first Treasury Secretary, and subject of a hit musical, appears on this bill.
Whose face is on it? US money by value.Andrew Jackson: Plans announced in 2016 would replace him with Harriet Tubman, but the redesign has been delayed.
Whose face is on it? US money by value.Ulysses S. Grant: Grant led the Union army to victory in 1865 before becoming the 18th president.
Whose face is on it? US money by value.Benjamin Franklin: Along with Hamilton, he is one of two non-presidents on current bills.

When these comedians joined the SNL cast.Chevy Chase: The first breakout star, famed for pratfalls and as first Weekend Update anchor, he left after a season and a half in 1976, leaving fans surprised.
When these comedians joined the SNL cast.Bill Murray: Joined in 1977 as a replacement for Chevy Chase, and went on to Ghostbusters, Groundhog Day and Lost in Translation, and is a frequent guest host.
When these comedians joined the SNL cast.Eddie Murphy: Joined at 19, and became a star with characters like Gumby and Buckwheat, and also the show's biggest hit of the early 1980s, helping rescue it.
When these comedians joined the SNL cast.Mike Myers: Joined in 1989, and created Wayne Campbell of "Wayne's World", a sketch that spun off into a hit movie in 1992, and later made Austin Powers.
When these comedians joined the SNL cast.Chris Farley: Joined in 1990 and became known for physical comedy, like the Chippendales sketch with Patrick Swayze. He died in 1997, at 33.
When these comedians joined the SNL cast.Will Ferrell: Joined in 1995, famous for his Harry Caray, George W. Bush and cowbell sketches, and later starred in Elf and Anchorman.
When these comedians joined the SNL cast.Tina Fey (on air): She joined as a writer in 1997, became head writer and Weekend Update anchor, and later turned her SNL experience into the sitcom 30 Rock.
When these comedians joined the SNL cast.Kristen Wiig: Joined in 2005 and known for her characters including Target Lady, Gilly and the Spanish-speaking Penelope, and she's also a star of Bridesmaids.
When these comedians joined the SNL cast.Kate McKinnon: Joined in 2012, and known for her impressions of Hillary Clinton and Ruth Bader Ginsburg, as well as Justin Bieber, and won Emmys for the show.
When these comedians joined the SNL cast.Pete Davidson: Joined in 2014 at age 20, one of the youngest cast members ever, and became known for his Weekend Update segments and blunt, self-mocking humor.

Supermarket staples, by launch year.Jell-O: The gelatin dessert was invented in 1897 in Le Roy, New York, and the town has a museum for it.
Supermarket staples, by launch year.Velveeta: Invented in Monroe, New York, in 1918, its name was meant to evoke velvet, and it melts smoothly thanks to added emulsifiers.
Supermarket staples, by launch year.Wonder Bread: Wonder Bread's colorful balloon logo was inspired by the sight of balloons at the Indianapolis Speedway, and it's now a baking icon.
Supermarket staples, by launch year.Kool-Aid: This powdered drink was invented by Edwin Perkins in Nebraska, and in 1998 it became the state's official soft drink.
Supermarket staples, by launch year.Spam: Hormel's canned pork arrived in 1937, and American troops in World War II ate millions of cans of it.
Supermarket staples, by launch year.Swanson TV dinner: Swanson reportedly had a mountain of leftover Thanksgiving turkey, and its answer was a frozen meal in a foil tray.
Supermarket staples, by launch year.Tang: This orange drink mix became linked to the space program after astronaut John Glenn drank it in orbit in 1962.
Supermarket staples, by launch year.Cool Whip: The whipped topping was introduced in 1966, and it is made from oil and water instead of cream.
Supermarket staples, by launch year.Lunchables: Oscar Mayer's lunch kits began in the late 1980s, and they carry crackers, cheese and meat in a tray.
Supermarket staples, by launch year.Impossible Burger: The plant-based burger launched in 2016 and uses a molecule called heme to mimic the flavor of meat.

Milestones of ancient and medieval medic.Earliest skull trepanations: Many of the skulls show signs of healing, so some patients survived.
Milestones of ancient and medieval medic.Hammurabi sets surgeons' fees: Its code set fees, and a surgeon whose patient died could lose his hands.
Milestones of ancient and medieval medic.Edwin Smith surgical papyrus: This Egyptian text describes 48 injuries rationally, with little magic.
Milestones of ancient and medieval medic.Hippocratic Oath: It does not contain 'First, do no harm', despite what many people think.
Milestones of ancient and medieval medic.Galen arrives in Rome: A doctor to gladiators and then an emperor, his animal-based anatomy errors held for 1,400 years.
Milestones of ancient and medieval medic.Avicenna's Canon of Medicine: Avicenna's book was a standard text in both Europe and the Islamic world for centuries.
Milestones of ancient and medieval medic.Mondino's public dissection: It was a public dissection at Bologna, and his anatomy manual was used for about 200 years.
Milestones of ancient and medieval medic.First quarantine (Ragusa): Modern Dubrovnik held ships for 30 days, later 40, the origin of the word 'quarantine'.
Milestones of ancient and medieval medic.Paré's book on gunshot wounds: The French barber-surgeon ran out of boiling oil and found that soothing ointment worked better.
Milestones of ancient and medieval medic.Leeuwenhoek sees bacteria: The Dutch draper built his own microscopes and called microbes 'animalcules'.

European lakes by surface area.Lake Bled: A tiny church sits on its island, and visitors ring a wishing bell inside. Bled's cream cake is as famous as the lake.
European lakes by surface area.Loch Lomond: It's the largest lake by surface area in Great Britain, and straddles the Highland Boundary Fault.
European lakes by surface area.Lake Garda: Italy's biggest lake has such a mild climate that lemons and olives grow along its shores, beneath the Alps.
European lakes by surface area.Lake Balaton: Central Europe's largest lake is very shallow, averaging just three metres or so, and warms up fast, so Hungarians call it their inland sea.
European lakes by surface area.Lake Inari: This Lapland lake is dotted with thousands of islands and is sacred to the Sámi, who have long fished its waters.
European lakes by surface area.Vättern: Its water is famously cold and clear. Each June thousands of cyclists ride a roughly 300 km loop around it in the Vätternrundan.
European lakes by surface area.Lake Peipus: It straddles the Estonia-Russia border, and in 1242 Alexander Nevsky's army defeated Teutonic knights on its ice.
European lakes by surface area.Vänern: Sweden's largest lake and the biggest in the European Union, it drains to the sea through the Göta river at Gothenburg.
European lakes by surface area.Lake Onega: Its islands include Kizhi, where a spectacular wooden church with 22 domes was built without a single nail.
European lakes by surface area.Lake Ladoga: Europe's largest lake. In the Siege of Leningrad, supplies crossed its frozen surface on the 'Road of Life'.

How many known species in each group?.Elephants: Scientists now split African elephants into two species, savanna and forest, alongside the Asian elephant.
How many known species in each group?.Bears: The giant panda is a true bear, and so is the polar bear, which is the largest land carnivore.
How many known species in each group?.Penguins: Nearly all live in the southern hemisphere, but the Galápagos penguin ranges right across the equator.
How many known species in each group?.Owls: Soft fringes on their wing feathers silence their flight, and their necks can rotate about 270 degrees.
How many known species in each group?.Sharks: They are older than trees, with fossils going back over 400 million years, and their skeletons are made of cartilage, not bone.
How many known species in each group?.Mammals: Rodents alone make up about 40 percent of all mammal species, and bats roughly one in five.
How many known species in each group?.Birds: Perching birds, from sparrows to crows, account for over half of all bird species.
How many known species in each group?.Spiders: All spiders make silk, but only some build webs. Many hunt by pouncing or ambush instead.
How many known species in each group?.Butterflies and moths: Moths outnumber butterflies by roughly nine to one, and most fly at night.
How many known species in each group?.Beetles: Biologist J. B. S. Haldane is said to have quipped that the Creator must have had 'an inordinate fondness for beetles'.

Typical weight of one of these fruits.Blueberry: A blueberry's dusty, waxy coating is natural and helps keep it from drying out. It is also why it looks silvery-blue.
Typical weight of one of these fruits.Grape: Most grapes are close to 80 percent water, and when dried they shrink into raisins, losing about three-quarters of their weight.
Typical weight of one of these fruits.Cherry: Cherries have a tiny stone, and one pit holds a seed that can sprout into a tree. Sour varieties are used for pies, sweet ones to eat fresh.
Typical weight of one of these fruits.Strawberry: A strawberry is not a true berry; its 'seeds' are actually separate tiny fruits on the outside, around 200 per fruit.
Typical weight of one of these fruits.Kiwi: Kiwis are native to China and were called Chinese gooseberries until New Zealand marketers renamed them after their national bird.
Typical weight of one of these fruits.Apple: Apples float because about a quarter of their volume is air, and they belong to the rose family along with pears and plums.
Typical weight of one of these fruits.Mango: Mango is the national fruit of India, and in some places the trees are so old and large that they may live for over a century.
Typical weight of one of these fruits.Pineapple: Pineapples contain bromelain, an enzyme that digests protein, which is why the fruit can make your mouth tingle as it eats you back.
Typical weight of one of these fruits.Watermelon: Watermelon is about 92 percent water, and it is a relative of the cucumber, pumpkin and squash, not of melons from the orchard.
Typical weight of one of these fruits.Jackfruit: The largest tree-borne fruit in the world, with spiny skin and a pungent smell, can weigh a lot more than this typical one.

Greek islands by area.Delos: This tiny rocky island is a sacred site in Greek mythology, the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis, and now an archaeological museum.
Greek islands by area.Santorini: The volcano island is famous for its white villages and whose huge eruption about 3,600 years ago possibly helped end the Minoans.
Greek islands by area.Naxos: The largest of the Cyclades is said to have been where Dionysus was raised, and it is known for its marble and potatoes.
Greek islands by area.Corfu: The island is a place that was ruled by Venice for centuries, and it helped inspire the writer Gerald Durrell's stories.
Greek islands by area.Kefalonia: The largest of the Ionian islands is home to loggerhead turtles and to a notorious sea cave known as Melissani.
Greek islands by area.Chios: The island is said to be the birthplace of Homer, and the main product of its mastic trees is a prized resin.
Greek islands by area.Rhodes: The island's Colossus was one of the Seven Wonders, and the Knights Hospitaller later ruled it.
Greek islands by area.Lesbos: The poet Sappho lived on this island, and the word lesbian is derived from its name.
Greek islands by area.Euboea: The island is the second largest, next to the mainland, and a bridge connects it to the mainland.
Greek islands by area.Crete: The largest Greek island was home to the Minoan civilisation, which built the palace of Knossos about 4,000 years ago.

How old these prehistoric treasures are.Lion-man figurine: Carved from mammoth ivory in a German cave, this figure has a human body and a cave lion's head, an early image of an imagined being.
How old these prehistoric treasures are.Chauvet Cave paintings: Found in France in 1994, its charcoal lions and rhinos were sealed by a rockfall for millennia, which kept them remarkably fresh.
How old these prehistoric treasures are.Venus of Willendorf: Only about 11 cm tall, this limestone figure was found in Austria in 1908 and still bears traces of red ochre paint.
How old these prehistoric treasures are.Lascaux cave paintings: Four teenagers found this French cave in 1940. It closed to the public in 1963 because visitors' breath was harming the paintings.
How old these prehistoric treasures are.Oldest known bread: Charred flatbread crumbs from Jordan's Black Desert show hunter-gatherers baked bread thousands of years before farming began.
How old these prehistoric treasures are.Shigir Idol: This carved larch post from a Russian peat bog once stood about 5 m tall, making it the oldest known large wooden sculpture.
How old these prehistoric treasures are.Carnac stones: Brittany holds thousands of standing stones in long, straight rows, and nobody knows for certain why they were raised.
How old these prehistoric treasures are.Ötzi the Iceman: Found frozen in the Alps in 1991, he carried a copper axe, and an arrowhead lodged in his shoulder probably killed him.
How old these prehistoric treasures are.Stonehenge (first phase): Its first phase was just a circular ditch and bank. The famous giant stones were added centuries afterwards.
How old these prehistoric treasures are.Nebra sky disc: Found in Germany, this bronze disc inlaid with gold sun, moon and stars may be the oldest concrete picture of the cosmos.

Average temperatures across the Solar Sy.Pluto: Pluto's heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice was revealed by the New Horizons flyby in 2015.
Average temperatures across the Solar Sy.Uranus (cloud tops): It is tilted on its side, so each pole gets decades of sunlight followed by decades of darkness.
Average temperatures across the Solar Sy.Titan: Saturn's biggest moon has a thick atmosphere, with methane lakes, rivers and rain.
Average temperatures across the Solar Sy.Saturn (cloud tops): Saturn is less dense than water, so in a giant enough bathtub it would float.
Average temperatures across the Solar Sy.Jupiter (cloud tops): The Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth that has raged for centuries.
Average temperatures across the Solar Sy.Mars: Near the equator it can reach about 20 °C by day, then plunge far below freezing at night.
Average temperatures across the Solar Sy.Earth: The only world known with liquid oceans on its surface, helped by an atmosphere that keeps it near this average.
Average temperatures across the Solar Sy.Mercury: Closest to the Sun but not the hottest, its nights drop to about -180 °C since there is no atmosphere to hold heat.
Average temperatures across the Solar Sy.Venus: A thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, making it hotter than Mercury and hot enough to melt lead.
Average temperatures across the Solar Sy.The Sun's surface: The surface is far cooler than the core, about 15 million °C, and the outer corona is hotter still, a long-standing puzzle.

Scientists who experimented on themselve.John Hunter and gonorrhea: The Scottish surgeon infected himself with what he thought was gonorrhea, but may have contracted syphilis, muddling his findings.
Scientists who experimented on themselve.Stubbins Ffirth drinks vomit: Ffirth drank vomit and bathed in the fluids of yellow fever patients to prove it wasn't contagious; he was wrong, mosquitoes spread it.
Scientists who experimented on themselve.Daniel Carrión and bartonella: The Peruvian medical student injected himself with blood from a wart and died of Oroya fever, proving the two diseases were one.
Scientists who experimented on themselve.Pettenkofer drinks cholera: He swallowed cholera bacteria to disprove germ theory and barely got ill, but the theory was right; he was just lucky.
Scientists who experimented on themselve.Jesse Lazear and yellow fever: Lazear let infected mosquitoes bite him and died of yellow fever, helping prove that mosquitoes carry the disease.
Scientists who experimented on themselve.Forssmann's heart catheter: Werner Forssmann threaded a catheter into his own heart via an arm vein, then walked to the X-ray room; he shared the 1956 Nobel Prize.
Scientists who experimented on themselve.Hofmann's LSD bicycle ride: After Albert Hofmann took LSD on purpose, he cycled home, and April 19 is now celebrated as Bicycle Day.
Scientists who experimented on themselve.Stapp's rocket sled: John Stapp rode a rocket sled from about 1,000 km/h to a stop in about 1.4 seconds, enduring around 46 g.
Scientists who experimented on themselve.Marshall drinks H. pylori: Barry Marshall drank H. pylori to show it causes stomach ulcers; he and Robin Warren won the 2005 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
Scientists who experimented on themselve.Kevin Warwick's chip implant: The British scientist had a chip implanted in his arm that operated doors and lights, and called himself the first cyborg.

When these 20th-century leaders took pow.Vladimir Lenin: The Bolsheviks seized power in the October Revolution, and Lenin led the world's first communist state until he died in 1924.
When these 20th-century leaders took pow.Benito Mussolini: He took power after the 1922 'March on Rome' and ruled as Il Duce until 1943.
When these 20th-century leaders took pow.Adolf Hitler: Appointed chancellor in January 1933, he used the Reichstag fire weeks later to seize emergency powers.
When these 20th-century leaders took pow.Francisco Franco: He won the Spanish Civil War and ruled until 1975; Spain returned to monarchy and democracy after his death.
When these 20th-century leaders took pow.Mao Zedong: He proclaimed the People's Republic from Tiananmen Gate on 1 October 1949.
When these 20th-century leaders took pow.Fidel Castro: His revolution toppled Batista; he ruled Cuba for decades, and handed power to his brother Raúl in 2008.
When these 20th-century leaders took pow.Muammar Gaddafi: A 27-year-old army officer when he seized Libya in a bloodless coup, he ruled for over 40 years until 2011.
When these 20th-century leaders took pow.Augusto Pinochet: He led the 1973 coup against Salvador Allende and ruled Chile until 1990.
When these 20th-century leaders took pow.Ayatollah Khomeini: Returning from exile in France in February 1979, he became Iran's Supreme Leader after the revolution.
When these 20th-century leaders took pow.Mikhail Gorbachev: His glasnost and perestroika reforms preceded the USSR's 1991 dissolution, and he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990.

Grams of sugar per liter.Brut Nature Champagne: Zero dosage means no added sugar, which makes it the driest style.
Grams of sugar per liter.Brut Champagne: 'Brut' means 'raw' or 'dry', and this is the most common style of the wine.
Grams of sugar per liter.Tomato juice: Tomato is botanically a fruit, though the US Supreme Court ruled it a vegetable for tariffs in 1893.
Grams of sugar per liter.Demi-sec Champagne: Despite 'demi-sec' meaning 'half-dry', it tastes distinctly sweet.
Grams of sugar per liter.Orange juice: It has about 8% sugar, close to a cola's level.
Grams of sugar per liter.Coca-Cola: A single 330 ml can holds about 35 grams of sugar, around nine teaspoons.
Grams of sugar per liter.Pedro Ximénez sherry: Made from sun-dried grapes, this sherry is so thick that it is often poured over ice cream.
Grams of sugar per liter.Sweetened condensed milk: Gail Borden developed it in 1856 to preserve milk, and the sugar acts as the preservative.
Grams of sugar per liter.Maple syrup: It takes roughly 40 litres of sap to boil down to one litre of syrup.
Grams of sugar per liter.Honey: Honey is mostly fructose and glucose, and it barely spoils; jars found in Egyptian tombs were still edible.

The smallest US states by total area.Rhode Island: You can drive across it in under an hour, and its winding coast gives it hundreds of miles of shoreline despite the tiny area.
The smallest US states by total area.Delaware: The first state to ratify the Constitution, in 1787, which earned it the nickname the First State and a place at the head of the line.
The smallest US states by total area.Connecticut: The Hartford Courant, founded in 1764, is the oldest continuously published newspaper in the United States, and it is based here.
The smallest US states by total area.New Jersey: The most densely populated state in the country, even though it is better known for its farms, shore and the nickname Garden State.
The smallest US states by total area.New Hampshire: Its motto is 'Live Free or Die', and it has no general sales tax. It also holds the first presidential primary every cycle.
The smallest US states by total area.Hawaii: The only US state made up entirely of islands, which sits in the middle of the Pacific, thousands of kilometres from the mainland.
The smallest US states by total area.Maryland: Land for Washington, DC, was originally carved out of Maryland and Virginia, and the Chesapeake Bay splits the state in two.
The smallest US states by total area.South Carolina: The first state to secede from the Union, in December 1860, and the Civil War's opening shots fell at Fort Sumter in Charleston harbor.
The smallest US states by total area.Maine: The only US state whose name is a single syllable, and it supplies most of America's lobster, with forest covering about 90 percent of it.
The smallest US states by total area.Kentucky: Mammoth Cave here is the longest known cave system in the world, with over 400 miles of mapped passages beneath the hills.

Longest main spans of suspension bridges.Brooklyn Bridge: It opened in 1883 as the world's longest suspension bridge, and Washington Roebling directed its construction from his sickbed.
Longest main spans of suspension bridges.Forth Road Bridge: Opened in 1964 beside the 1890 Forth Rail Bridge in Scotland, its cables later corroded, prompting a replacement.
Longest main spans of suspension bridges.George Washington Bridge: Opened in 1931, its span nearly doubled the record at the time.
Longest main spans of suspension bridges.Mackinac Bridge: Called 'Mighty Mac', it joins Michigan's two peninsulas, and is about 8 km long in total.
Longest main spans of suspension bridges.Golden Gate Bridge: Opened in 1937, its color is called International Orange, chosen for visibility in fog.
Longest main spans of suspension bridges.Tsing Ma Bridge: It carries both road and rail traffic to Hong Kong's airport.
Longest main spans of suspension bridges.Humber Bridge: It was the world's longest single span when opened in 1981, holding the record for 16 years.
Longest main spans of suspension bridges.Great Belt East Bridge: It links Denmark's islands of Zealand and Funen, and opened in 1998.
Longest main spans of suspension bridges.Akashi Kaikyō Bridge: It held the record for 23 years, and the 1995 Kobe earthquake lengthened it by about a metre.
Longest main spans of suspension bridges.Çanakkale Bridge, Turkey: It crosses the Dardanelles, opening in 2022 as the longest; the span of 2,023 m nods to 2023's centenary.

Bestsellers of recent decades, by public.Bridget Jones's Diary: Helen Fielding's comic novel began as a newspaper column in The Independent and loosely retold Pride and Prejudice with a modern single woman.
Bestsellers of recent decades, by public.Harry Potter (book 1): The first book sold in the millions worldwide, and J.K. Rowling's publisher initially printed only about 500 hardcover copies.
Bestsellers of recent decades, by public.Life of Pi: Yann Martel's shipwreck tale about a boy and a Bengal tiger won the Booker Prize and later became an Oscar-winning film directed by Ang Lee.
Bestsellers of recent decades, by public.The Da Vinci Code: Dan Brown's thriller sold tens of millions of copies and sparked a wave of tourism to the Louvre and Rosslyn Chapel.
Bestsellers of recent decades, by public.Girl with the Dragon Tattoo: Swedish journalist Stieg Larsson died before any of his Millennium trilogy was published, never seeing its worldwide success.
Bestsellers of recent decades, by public.The Hunger Games: Suzanne Collins reportedly got the idea while flipping between reality TV and war coverage; the series became a defining young-adult dystopia.
Bestsellers of recent decades, by public.The Help: Kathryn Stockett's novel about Black maids in 1960s Mississippi was rejected by dozens of literary agents before it became a huge hit.
Bestsellers of recent decades, by public.Fifty Shades of Grey: E. L. James began this story as Twilight fan fiction, and it became one of the fastest-selling paperbacks in publishing history.
Bestsellers of recent decades, by public.Gone Girl: Gillian Flynn's thriller about a vanishing wife popularized the phrase 'cool girl' and was adapted into a 2014 David Fincher film.
Bestsellers of recent decades, by public.Where the Crawdads Sing: Delia Owens's debut novel, set in the North Carolina marshes, spent years on bestseller lists when she was in her seventies.

Radiation doses, from harmless to deadly.Eating a banana: Bananas hold radioactive potassium-40, which is why the 'banana equivalent dose' is a joking unit for radiation.
Radiation doses, from harmless to deadly.Dental X-ray: The dose is less than a day of natural background radiation, and a lead apron keeps it away from the rest of the body.
Radiation doses, from harmless to deadly.Chest X-ray: It equals only about two or three days of the radiation you absorb naturally from rocks, the air and space.
Radiation doses, from harmless to deadly.New York to LA flight: Cosmic rays are stronger at altitude, so airline crews get more radiation over a career than most office workers.
Radiation doses, from harmless to deadly.Mammogram: The dose equals roughly seven weeks of background radiation, a small risk set against the cancers it can catch early.
Radiation doses, from harmless to deadly.A year of natural background: The biggest natural contributor is radon, a gas that seeps up from rocks and collects in buildings.
Radiation doses, from harmless to deadly.Chest CT scan: One scan equals about two years of natural background, which is why doctors weigh scans carefully.
Radiation doses, from harmless to deadly.Nuclear worker yearly limit: In most countries, radiation workers are limited to about 20 mSv a year averaged over five years, with 50 mSv the cap in any one year.
Radiation doses, from harmless to deadly.Radiation sickness begins: Acute doses at this level cause nausea and fatigue, but the same amount spread over a lifetime is far less harmful.
Radiation doses, from harmless to deadly.Likely fatal dose: A short, whole-body dose like this kills about half of those exposed without medical treatment, so timing matters as much as amount.

First flights of Airbus models.Airbus A300: This was the first Airbus ever built, and the first twin-engine widebody airliner.
First flights of Airbus models.Airbus A310: It was a shorter A300 with a new wing, aimed at medium-length routes.
First flights of Airbus models.Airbus A320: This was the first airliner with digital fly-by-wire controls, replacing cables with computers.
First flights of Airbus models.Airbus A340: It had four engines for long routes, before regulators allowed twin-engine jets to cross oceans freely.
First flights of Airbus models.Airbus A330: It shares its wing design with the A340 but with two engines, and it eventually outsold its sibling.
First flights of Airbus models.Airbus A321: A stretched A320, long the biggest of the A320 family, used on busy short routes.
First flights of Airbus models.Airbus A319: A shortened A320, also made in a private-jet version.
First flights of Airbus models.Airbus A318: The smallest Airbus jet, nicknamed the Baby Bus, never sold as well as its bigger siblings.
First flights of Airbus models.Airbus A380: With two full-length decks, it is the largest passenger airliner ever built, and production ended after 251 aircraft.
First flights of Airbus models.Airbus A350: More than half of its structure is made of carbon fibre composites, lighter than the aluminium used for decades.

Distance from Rio de Janeiro.São Paulo: Brazil's largest city by far and its financial heartland, with a metro area of over 20 million people.
Distance from Rio de Janeiro.Brasília: Built from scratch and inaugurated in 1960 to replace Rio as capital; its layout is often said to resemble an airplane.
Distance from Rio de Janeiro.Buenos Aires: Home of tango, which it shares with Montevideo across the Rio de la Plata; its 9 de Julio Avenue is among the widest in the world.
Distance from Rio de Janeiro.Santiago, Chile: Chile's capital sits in a valley beneath the snowy Andes, so ski slopes lie within an hour or two of downtown.
Distance from Rio de Janeiro.Lima: A desert city on the Pacific that gets almost no rain, yet it holds about 10 million people and is famed for its cuisine.
Distance from Rio de Janeiro.Cape Town: Across the South Atlantic, its Table Mountain often wears a cloud called the tablecloth, and it sits at a latitude much like Rio's.
Distance from Rio de Janeiro.Lisbon: Portugal's royal court fled here from Napoleon to Rio in 1808, making Rio the capital of the Portuguese empire for years.
Distance from Rio de Janeiro.London: Rio sits three or four hours behind it, and the Greenwich meridian that sets world time runs through its suburbs.
Distance from Rio de Janeiro.Moscow: Russia's capital has a metro, opened in 1935, with ornate stations often called underground palaces.
Distance from Rio de Janeiro.Tokyo: Brazil is home to the largest Japanese population outside Japan, mostly in and around São Paulo, which is why the two feel oddly linked.

The Beaufort wind scale, from still to w.Calm: Smoke rises straight up and the sea is mirror-smooth; Admiral Francis Beaufort devised the scale in 1805 from observations at sea.
The Beaufort wind scale, from still to w.Light air: Smoke drifts and ripples form on water, but wind vanes don't yet move; speeds are about 1 to 3 knots.
The Beaufort wind scale, from still to w.Gentle breeze: Leaves and small twigs are in constant motion and a light flag stretches out; about 7 to 10 knots.
The Beaufort wind scale, from still to w.Moderate breeze: Wind lifts dust and loose paper and shakes small branches, a familiar force on a bright, blustery day.
The Beaufort wind scale, from still to w.Fresh breeze: Small leafy trees begin to sway and crested wavelets appear on lakes, and small craft sailors take note.
The Beaufort wind scale, from still to w.Near gale: Whole trees sway and walking against the wind becomes tiring, with speeds of about 28 to 33 knots.
The Beaufort wind scale, from still to w.Gale: It snaps twigs off trees and makes walking hard; forecasters begin issuing formal gale warnings at about 34 to 40 knots.
The Beaufort wind scale, from still to w.Strong gale: It can damage roofs by dislodging chimney pots and slates, with winds of about 41 to 47 knots.
The Beaufort wind scale, from still to w.Violent storm: Widespread damage is typical and it is rarely experienced on land; sea waves can reach about 10 to 12 m.
The Beaufort wind scale, from still to w.Hurricane force: Winds of 64 knots or more, around 118 km/h; the scale originally stopped at 12 and extra levels were added later for tropical cyclones.

Science fiction novels, by publication.The Time Machine: H.G. Wells popularized the phrase time machine, and sent his traveler to a far future of Eloi and Morlocks.
Science fiction novels, by publication.The War of the Worlds: A 1938 radio dramatization by Orson Welles reportedly frightened some listeners who thought the invasion was real.
Science fiction novels, by publication.I, Robot: Asimov's story collection explored the Three Laws of Robotics, which he wrote years before giving the book its name.
Science fiction novels, by publication.Foundation: Asimov modeled his galactic empire on Gibbon's Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire; Apple TV+ adapted it in 2021.
Science fiction novels, by publication.Stranger in a Strange Land: Robert Heinlein's novel gave English the verb grok, meaning to understand something deeply.
Science fiction novels, by publication.Dune: Frank Herbert's desert-planet epic is often cited as the best-selling science fiction novel, and it is built on ecology.
Science fiction novels, by publication.The Left Hand of Darkness: Ursula K. Le Guin imagined a world where people have no fixed sex; it won both the Hugo and Nebula awards.
Science fiction novels, by publication.The Hitchhiker's Guide: It began as a BBC radio comedy in 1978; its supercomputer's answer to life, the universe and everything is 42.
Science fiction novels, by publication.Neuromancer: William Gibson's novel popularized cyberspace and launched cyberpunk, winning the Hugo, Nebula and Philip K. Dick awards.
Science fiction novels, by publication.The Martian: Andy Weir posted it free online in chapters, then self-published it on Kindle before a publisher bought it.

When these chicken chains were founded.KFC: Harland Sanders, an honorary colonel, began selling chicken in a Kentucky roadside station; the first franchise opened in Utah in 1952.
When these chicken chains were founded.Chick-fil-A: Truett Cathy created the chicken sandwich in Georgia; the chain stays closed on Sundays.
When these chicken chains were founded.Popeyes: Named for Popeye Doyle in The French Connection, not the sailor, it brought spicy New Orleans-style chicken to the world.
When these chicken chains were founded.El Pollo Loco: Spanish for the crazy chicken, it began as a roadside stand in Guasave, Sinaloa, Mexico.
When these chicken chains were founded.Bojangles: A Southern chain from Charlotte known for Cajun-seasoned chicken and buttermilk biscuits.
When these chicken chains were founded.Nando's: Peri-peri chicken with Portuguese-Mozambican roots started in Johannesburg, South Africa.
When these chicken chains were founded.Zaxby's: Founded in Statesboro, Georgia by two friends named Zach and Tony.
When these chicken chains were founded.Wingstop: Started in Garland, Texas, and specializes in wings with dozens of sauce flavors.
When these chicken chains were founded.Raising Cane's: Named after the founder's yellow Labrador, Cane, and built around chicken fingers.
When these chicken chains were founded.Dave's Hot Chicken: It began as a Los Angeles parking-lot pop-up and sold to Roark Capital for a reported $1 billion.

The early Space Race, month by month.Sputnik 1: Beach-ball sized and 58 cm wide, its radio beeps shocked the world for three weeks.
The early Space Race, month by month.Laika aboard Sputnik 2: A Moscow street dog was the first animal to orbit Earth, and she did not survive.
The early Space Race, month by month.Explorer 1: America's first satellite discovered the Van Allen radiation belts.
The early Space Race, month by month.NASA opens for business: It grew out of the older NACA and began work on October 1.
The early Space Race, month by month.Pioneer 4 passes the Moon: The first US probe to escape Earth's gravity, it passed the Moon at 60,000 km, missing its target.
The early Space Race, month by month.Luna 2 hits the Moon: The first human-made object to reach another world, it deliberately crashed carrying Soviet pennants.
The early Space Race, month by month.Gagarin orbits Earth: He shouted Poyekhali, Let's go, at launch, and was out of orbit in 108 minutes.
The early Space Race, month by month.Shepard's suborbital hop: Alan Shepard's Freedom 7 flight lasted only 15 minutes.
The early Space Race, month by month.JFK's Moon challenge: Kennedy told Congress America should land a man on the Moon before the decade's end.
The early Space Race, month by month.Titov's full day in orbit: Gherman Titov was 25, still the youngest person to fly in space, and the first to sleep in orbit.

Pieces in a full set.Yahtzee dice: Entrepreneur Edwin Lowe bought the game from a couple who played it on their yacht, which is why it was originally called Yacht.
Pieces in a full set.Checkers: Each side starts with 12 pieces. Computer scientists 'solved' the game in 2007: perfect play always ends in a draw.
Pieces in a full set.Double-six dominoes: Every pairing from blank-blank to six-six appears exactly once. The game reached Europe, probably via Italy, in the 1700s.
Pieces in a full set.Chess: Each side has 16 pieces. The number of possible chess games is estimated to dwarf the atoms in the observable universe.
Pieces in a full set.Connect Four discs: Six rows by seven columns. It was solved in 1988: with perfect play, the first player can always win.
Pieces in a full set.Deck of cards (no jokers): A well-shuffled deck is almost certainly in an order never seen before: 52 cards can be arranged in about 8 followed by 67 zeros ways.
Pieces in a full set.Tarot deck: Tarot has 22 major and 56 minor cards. It began in 15th-century Italy as a card game called tarocchi, long before fortune-telling.
Pieces in a full set.Scrabble tiles (English): Inventor Alfred Butts set the letter counts by tallying letters on the front page of the New York Times. Two tiles are blank.
Pieces in a full set.Mahjong tiles: Tiles come in three suits plus winds, dragons, flowers and seasons. It is often compared to a rummy-style card game.
Pieces in a full set.Go stones: The 361 matches the 19-by-19 intersections of the board. Go is over 2,500 years old and has vastly more positions than chess.

One hit single for each year of the 1990.Nothing Compares 2 U: Prince wrote it, but Sinéad O'Connor's version topped charts worldwide, with a video that is one tearful close-up.
One hit single for each year of the 1990.Losing My Religion: R.E.M.'s mandolin-led hit takes its title from a Southern phrase meaning being at the end of your rope.
One hit single for each year of the 1990.I Will Always Love You: Dolly Parton wrote it, and Whitney Houston's version for The Bodyguard spent 14 weeks at number one in the US.
One hit single for each year of the 1990.What's Up? (4 Non Blondes): Linda Perry's belting chorus asks 'what's going on?'; she later wrote hits like Pink's 'Get the Party Started'.
One hit single for each year of the 1990.Zombie (The Cranberries): Dolores O'Riordan wrote it after an IRA bombing in Warrington in 1993 killed two children.
One hit single for each year of the 1990.Gangsta's Paradise: Coolio built it on a Stevie Wonder sample from 'Pastime Paradise', and it was written for the film Dangerous Minds.
One hit single for each year of the 1990.Wannabe: The Spice Girls' debut single hit number one in over 30 countries.
One hit single for each year of the 1990.Barbie Girl: Aqua's Danish-Norwegian hit prompted Mattel to sue, and the toymaker lost.
One hit single for each year of the 1990.Believe (Cher): Its robotic voice effect came from pushing Auto-Tune to extremes, and the sound is nicknamed the 'Cher effect'.
One hit single for each year of the 1990.Livin' la Vida Loca: Ricky Martin's blazing 1999 Grammy performance helped set off the Latin pop boom.

From paddy to plate: rice.Plough and flood the paddy: Rice is often grown in paddies, flooded fields that suppress weeds. Water buffalo have long pulled the ploughs across Asia's wet fields.
From paddy to plate: rice.Plant seedlings by hand: Seedlings are raised in a nursery bed and then transplanted in neat rows. It is back-breaking work, often done by hand.
From paddy to plate: rice.Rice grows in the water: Rice is one of the few major crops that tolerates standing water. Its stems carry air down to the roots, so it does not drown.
From paddy to plate: rice.Drain the field: Farmers let the field dry before harvest so the ground firms up. The plants ripen and turn golden at this stage.
From paddy to plate: rice.Cut the ripe stalks: Harvest takes place about three to six months after planting, depending on variety. Many farmers still cut the stalks with a sickle.
From paddy to plate: rice.Thresh out the grains: Threshing separates the grains from the stalks, by beating them or using a machine. The leftover straw is used for thatch, feed and bedding.
From paddy to plate: rice.Dry the grains in the sun: Grains must be dried to the right moisture for storage. Spread on mats or roads, the drying rice can colour the landscape golden.
From paddy to plate: rice.Mill off the husks: The tough outer husk is removed to give brown rice, which keeps its bran. The husks themselves can be burned as fuel or used in packing.
From paddy to plate: rice.Polish into white rice: Polishing strips off the bran and germ, leaving white rice. It stores longer, but also loses some vitamins, which once caused beriberi.
From paddy to plate: rice.Cook and serve: Rice feeds more than half the world's population. In many Asian languages, the word for cooked rice is also the word for a meal.

Ways to travel, by when they were invent.Wheeled cart: The earliest known wheel with an axle was found in Slovenia, dating to about 3150 BC; early wheels were also used for pottery.
Ways to travel, by when they were invent.Chariot: Spoked-wheel chariots appeared around 2000 BC on the Eurasian steppe, and the lighter wheel made war chariots fast and agile.
Ways to travel, by when they were invent.Hot air balloon: The first passengers in the Montgolfier brothers' 1783 balloon were a sheep, a duck and a rooster, not people.
Ways to travel, by when they were invent.Steam locomotive: Richard Trevithick's steam locomotive hauled iron and men along a Welsh tramway in 1804, decades before passenger railways.
Ways to travel, by when they were invent.Bicycle (no pedals yet): Karl Drais's 1817 machine had no pedals, so riders pushed along the ground with their feet, and it was nicknamed the hobby horse.
Ways to travel, by when they were invent.Petrol car: Karl Benz patented his motorwagen in 1886, and his wife Bertha made the first long-distance trip in it in 1888 to prove it worked.
Ways to travel, by when they were invent.Airplane: The Wright brothers' first powered flight on December 17, 1903 lasted about 12 seconds and covered roughly 37 metres.
Ways to travel, by when they were invent.Helicopter: The first practical helicopters flew in the late 1930s, though earlier machines in the 1900s had barely left the ground.
Ways to travel, by when they were invent.Jet airliner: The de Havilland Comet, which first flew in 1949, was the first jet airliner, though early metal fatigue problems grounded it.
Ways to travel, by when they were invent.Crewed spacecraft: Yuri Gagarin's Vostok 1 flight in 1961 lasted 108 minutes and made him the first human in space.

Nobel laureates, by year they won.Wilhelm Röntgen: He won the first Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering X-rays, and refused to patent them so everyone could benefit.
Nobel laureates, by year they won.Marie Curie: She shared the physics prize for radioactivity and won chemistry in 1911, remaining the only person to win in two different sciences.
Nobel laureates, by year they won.Albert Einstein: His prize cited the photoelectric effect, not relativity, which the committee still considered too controversial.
Nobel laureates, by year they won.Winston Churchill: His Nobel was in literature, for historical and biographical writing and brilliant oratory, not for peace.
Nobel laureates, by year they won.Ernest Hemingway: He was recovering from two plane crashes in Africa and could not travel to Stockholm to collect the prize.
Nobel laureates, by year they won.Mother Teresa: The Peace Prize honoured her work with the poor in Kolkata, and she asked that the banquet money go to the needy; she was declared a saint in 2016.
Nobel laureates, by year they won.Nelson Mandela: He shared the Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk for ending apartheid peacefully, and became South Africa's first Black president a year later.
Nobel laureates, by year they won.Barack Obama: He received the Peace Prize less than a year into his presidency, which surprised many, citing his diplomacy and outreach.
Nobel laureates, by year they won.Malala Yousafzai: At 17 she became the youngest Nobel laureate ever, having survived a Taliban shooting for campaigning for girls' education.
Nobel laureates, by year they won.Bob Dylan: He was the first musician to win the literature prize, honoured for new poetic expressions within the American song tradition.

Old approximations of π.The Bible's 1 Kings: A Bible verse describing Solomon's basin gives a circle with circumference 30 and diameter 10, which implies pi is 3.
Old approximations of π.Babylonian tablet: A clay tablet from about 1900 to 1600 BC uses 25/8, or 3.125, in circle problems.
Old approximations of π.Archimedes, lower bound: Using polygons of 96 sides, Archimedes trapped pi between two fractions; this lower bound is 223/71.
Old approximations of π.Zu Chongzhi: The Chinese mathematician's fraction 355/113 stayed the most accurate approximation for nearly a thousand years.
Old approximations of π.Aryabhata: The Indian astronomer called his value approximate, hinting that pi cannot be written exactly.
Old approximations of π.Ptolemy: The Almagest astronomer used 3;8,30 in base-60 notation, which is about 3.1417.
Old approximations of π.Fibonacci: In his geometry book, he gave 864/275, about 3.1418, though he's better known for numerals and rabbits.
Old approximations of π.Archimedes, upper bound: This upper bound is 22/7, still a common school approximation, celebrated on July 22 as Pi Approximation Day.
Old approximations of π.Egyptian Rhind papyrus: The scribe Ahmes copied this papyrus about 1650 BC, using a rule equal to (16/9) squared.
Old approximations of π.Brahmagupta: The Indian mathematician used the square root of 10 for pi, and also set out the rules for arithmetic with zero.

Colonial America, from Jamestown on.Jamestown founded: Founded by the Virginia Company, the colonists suffered a starving time, and tobacco later saved the colony.
Colonial America, from Jamestown on.Mayflower voyage: About 102 passengers sailed, landing at Cape Cod, where they signed the Mayflower Compact.
Colonial America, from Jamestown on.Boston founded: Puritan John Winthrop founded it and called the colony a city upon a hill.
Colonial America, from Jamestown on.Harvard founded: America's oldest university is named after its first benefactor, John Harvard.
Colonial America, from Jamestown on.Pennsylvania chartered: William Penn received it from Charles II to settle a debt to his father, and it became a haven for Quakers.
Colonial America, from Jamestown on.Salem witch trials: Twenty people were executed in the Massachusetts witch trials, and the frenzy ended when the governor intervened.
Colonial America, from Jamestown on.Yale founded: Founded in Connecticut and later moved to New Haven, it is named after benefactor Elihu Yale.
Colonial America, from Jamestown on.Stamp Act: A British tax on printed paper that sparked the cry of no taxation without representation.
Colonial America, from Jamestown on.Declaration of Independence: Thomas Jefferson drafted it, and it was adopted on July 4 and signed mostly in August.
Colonial America, from Jamestown on.Treaty of Paris: Britain recognised American independence, ending the Revolutionary War.

Chinese firsts and landmarks.Silk: Legend credits Empress Leizu with discovering silk when a cocoon dropped into her tea, and China guarded the secret for thousands of years.
Chinese firsts and landmarks.Kites: Early Chinese kites were used by the military to carry messages and measure distances, long before people flew them for fun.
Chinese firsts and landmarks.Great Wall begun under Qin: The wall most visitors see today is mainly from the Ming dynasty; earlier walls were largely rammed earth and are mostly gone.
Chinese firsts and landmarks.Silk Road opened: Emperor Wu of Han sent the envoy Zhang Qian west, and the route he opened eventually linked China to the Roman world.
Chinese firsts and landmarks.Paper (Cai Lun): Court official Cai Lun is credited with improving paper-making using bark, rags and fishing nets, though earlier paper exists.
Chinese firsts and landmarks.Zhang Heng's seismoscope: This bronze vessel with dragon heads dropped a ball from a dragon's mouth into a toad's when it sensed a distant earthquake.
Chinese firsts and landmarks.Diamond Sutra printed: The world's oldest dated printed book was found in a sealed cave in Dunhuang and is now kept in the British Library.
Chinese firsts and landmarks.First paper money: Sichuan merchants' paper notes were replaced by government-backed ones under the Song, centuries before Europe printed banknotes.
Chinese firsts and landmarks.Movable type: Bi Sheng carved characters in clay, centuries before Gutenberg, but thousands of Chinese characters made the system impractical.
Chinese firsts and landmarks.Magnetic compass at sea: Chinese texts describe sailors steering with a magnetized needle by this era, which later spread to the Islamic world and Europe.
